headline: Viagogo Unveils Revolutionary Pricing Model Called 'Lying'
subheadline: *UK watchdog provisionally finds the ticket reseller's drip pricing may break the law; customers nationwide realise the surprise fees were not a loyalty minigame.*
author: Felicity Brandt, Consumer Regret Desk
seoTitle: Viagogo's Hidden Fees May Be Illegal, UK Watchdog Finds
seoDescription: Satire: The UK's competition watchdog provisionally found Viagogo's drip pricing may break the law. Customers had assumed the mystery fees were a rewards scheme.
sourceEvent: The UK's Competition and Markets Authority has provisionally found that ticket-reselling site Viagogo may have broken consumer protection law by using drip pricing — advertising a low headline price before adding mandatory fees at checkout. The finding is part of a wider crackdown on hidden charges under new consumer powers.

social.x: The CMA says Viagogo's hidden fees may be illegal. This is devastating news for the thousands of customers who believed the mystery charges were a fun loyalty game they were slowly winning.
social.facebook: The UK's competition watchdog has provisionally found that Viagogo's drip pricing — where a £60 ticket becomes £112 via a service fee, a booking fee, and a 'fee fee' — may break consumer law. The news has devastated loyal customers, many of whom had spent years collecting the surprise fees in the belief they would eventually be redeemable for a tote bag.
social.linkedin: The CMA's provisional finding on Viagogo's drip pricing is a reminder that transparency is not a premium add-on — although, to be fair, Viagogo does charge one. Analysis of what this means for checkout UX, consumer trust, and the emerging 'fee fee' category below.

altHeadlines: Watchdog Probes Ticket Site After Realising '£60' Was More of a Suggestion
Viagogo Introduces Fee for Discovering Its Other Fees

body:
LONDON — The Competition and Markets Authority has provisionally found that ticket-reselling site Viagogo may have broken consumer protection law through 'drip pricing,' the innovative business model in which a £60 concert ticket gradually reveals itself to cost £112 via a service fee, a booking fee, a delivery fee for a ticket that is not delivered, and a fourth fee economists believe is for vibes.

The finding has come as a profound shock to consumers, many of whom had spent years paying the mystery charges in the sincere belief they were accumulating points in an elaborate loyalty programme.

'Every time I checked out there was a new fee, and honestly I thought I was levelling up,' said local man Darren Pegg, 38, who estimates he has unlocked approximately £2,400 in 'rewards' since 2019. 'I was waiting for the little pop-up that said congratulations. It turns out the pop-up was the invoice.'

Viagogo defended its practices, noting that all fees are technically disclosed — in light grey four-point type, once per customer, in a location the company describes as 'on the website, somewhere.'

'Transparency is a core value at Viagogo,' a company spokesperson said. 'Which is why we're proud to disclose that this statement costs £4.99 to read, plus a £12 statement-processing fee and a £3.50 transparency surcharge.'

The CMA's provisional findings reportedly include a 'mandatory optional fee,' a charge for using the website that charges for using the website, and a small item listed only as 'mystery,' which one analyst described as 'the most honest line item in British commerce.'

'The genius of drip pricing is that by the time customers see the real total, they are too emotionally invested in the checkout process to leave,' said one consumer economist. 'It is the sunk-cost fallacy with a basket icon.'

In response to the investigation, Viagogo has announced a new simplified pricing structure consisting of a single transparent 'everything fee,' calculated by spinning a large wheel, and a premium 'no surprises' tier that surprises you in advance.

At press time, the CMA confirmed its provisional finding itself had been subject to a £14.99 provisional-finding convenience charge, VAT, and a £6 'watchdog administration fee,' which the authority has decided, on reflection, to also provisionally find illegal.
